title: Your others rule
hookLine: one page for people: the Mohists said love everyone without distinction; Mencius said love starts at home and widens
tomorrow: what did Augustine hear a child chanting over the garden wall?

lines: YI ZHI: LOVE HAS NO DEGREES.
cards: A nephew's school play, or a stranger's fundraiser across town. Most weeks, someone is choosing. In ancient China, two schools fought about exactly that.

A follower of Mozi named Yi Zhi taught that love should have no degrees. And Mencius, the Confucian teacher, sent back a question: does he really think a man loves his brother's child no more than a neighbor's baby?

teach.b: View one, the Mohists. Their teacher, Mozi, argued for love without distinction. Look at where harm comes from, he said.
People rob other families because they love only their own. States attack other states for the same reason. If everyone regarded other people's families as their own, who would harm anyone?
Partiality is where the damage starts. That's the strongest case, and it's a serious one. View two, Mencius.
He told a story about the oldest times. Some people didn't bury their parents; they left the bodies in a ditch.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: SWEAT ON THEIR FOREHEADS.
teach.b: Later, passing by, they saw the animals at them, and sweat broke out on their foreheads. Nobody made them feel that. It came from inside.
They went home for baskets and spades. For Mencius, that's the root: love really does start nearest, with family, and then you extend it.
Treat the elders in your own family with reverence, he told a king, and carry that out to the elders of others.
Confucian teaching calls it love with an order: begin at home, then widen the circle. Both schools wanted a kinder world. They disagreed about where love starts.
Your others rule can hold both: name your people, and leave room on the page for the widening.

how: Confucian teaching begins love with family and extends it outward; the Mohists argued for love without distinction. A rule of life can keep a page that names your people and the wider circle you reach toward.

o: a list of everyone you've decided to stop helping
a promise to treat every stranger exactly like family
one page naming your people and the wider circle beyond

s: Mencius taught that love should stay inside the family
he taught extending it: reverence for your own elders, carried out to the elders of others.
Mozi argued that partiality is where harm between families and states starts
if everyone regarded others' families as their own, who would harm anyone?
the Mohists said family doesn't matter at all
they argued against loving only your own, not against loving family.

games.q: your friend says loving your own family more is just favoritism. give the Mohist's best case.
o: harm starts when people love only their own; treat others' families as yours and no one is harmed.
family ties are a trap and should be left behind for the sake of the world.
love is a feeling, so it can't be taught or widened at all.
games.why: Mozi traced theft and war to partiality. Mencius answered that love really does start nearest, then extends.

practice: Draw a small circle and write two or three of your people inside it. Around it, draw a wider ring, and write one person or group beyond them you could reach toward.
For the rest of the sit, let your attention move slowly from the center out to the edge.

wordCard.voice: Your others rule: one page for people, your own named first, with a wider ring for the people beyond them.

carryVoice: Your line: my people. Mencius started at home, and Mozi wouldn't stop at the door. The others are all on one page now.
